h1:
Breakfast Like a Hat Yai Local
Dim Sum, Chicken Rice, Congee & Kopi
intro: Hat Yai is a town that wakes up early to eat. Locals are up before sunrise to grab a seat at a dim sum shop, go head-to-head over old-school chicken rice, or slurp hot congee with a sock-brewed cup of kopi. Breakfast here carries the Hokkien-Cantonese Chinese flavours of the south, mixed with a border-town feel that leans toward Malaysia. We've pulled together real shops, real neighbourhoods, rough prices, and opening hours so you can eat your way through the whole trip — picked from reviews, not places we sat down at ourselves.

blocks.html: Sleep in here and you'll miss the most fun meal of the day, because the best shops start selling from around 5:30–6am and many sell out before noon. Hat Yai's breakfast culture revolves around three main things: dim sum, where you sip tea and chat for ages; chicken rice from old-timers who've sold it for generations; and congee with traditional coffee in old shophouses, plus morning markets you can graze through all morning. We'll walk you through each category.

blocks.text: 10 Breakfast Spots Hat Yai Locals Actually Go To

blocks.html: Ranked by how long they've been around, how popular they are, and how consistent the reviews are — not a final verdict on who's tastier, because each shop is strong at something different. Prices and times are rough estimates, so double-check with the shop before you go.

items.name: Chokdee Tae Tiam
items.blurb: The legendary Hat Yai dim sum shop everyone stops by. Dozens of freshly steamed baskets — har gow, siu mai, bao, braised pork leg — and packed from before dawn. Locals call this the face of Hat Yai dim sum.
items.meta: Dim sum · open early–late morning · downtown Hat Yai

items.name: Gook Chai Dim Sum
items.blurb: An old dim sum shop of 20-plus years on Thung Sao Road, near Central Hat Yai. Steamed dim sum, siu mai, bao, plus pork noodles if you want more. Locals are regulars and the morning buzz is the real deal.
items.meta: Dim sum · open ~6am–1pm · Thung Sao 1 Rd

items.name: Go Yong Chicken Rice
items.blurb: The first chicken rice shop in Hat Yai, going strong for close to a hundred years on Kim Pradit Road. Tender chicken, fragrant oily rice, and a punchy fermented-soybean dipping sauce. Plenty of locals have eaten here since childhood.
items.meta: Chicken rice · open early–late morning · Kim Pradit Rd

items.name: Thung Lung Chicken Rice
items.blurb: An old chicken rice shop open since 1955, using free-range chicken boiled until the meat is just-tender with springy skin, served with fragrant oily rice. Known across Hat Yai and Songkhla — worth a stop if you're passing through Thung Lung.
items.meta: Chicken rice · open mornings · Thung Lung area

items.name: Natt Coffee & Dim Sum
items.blurb: Fresh steamed dim sum and coffee in one place, near Saeng Thong School on Chi Uthit Road. They steam all day, so the whole shop smells of it. Good if you want hot baskets and a single cup of coffee, done.
items.meta: Dim sum + coffee · open ~6am–11:30am daily · Chi Uthit Rd
items.price: tens of baht per basket · ~100-ish THB per person

items.name: Ama Dim Sum
items.blurb: A dim sum shop on Thamnoon Withi Road, recently refreshed, with a comfortable sit-down feel and a big dim sum menu. Known for its braised pork leg. Open longer Thursday–Sunday than on weekdays — good if you'd rather relax than fight for a table.
items.meta: Dim sum · open ~6am–12:30pm (longer Thu–Sun) · Thamnoon Withi Rd

items.name: Lung Chok Congee & Soup (Kho Hong)
items.blurb: A morning shop in the Kho Hong area on Kanchanawanit Road, known for hot congee and pork-blood noodle soup — warm, filling, and easy on the wallet. Good if you want to start the day with something hot to slurp instead of dim sum.
items.meta: Congee/soup · open ~6am–10:30am daily · Kanchanawanit Rd, Kho Hong

items.name: Je Chada Traditional Coffee
items.blurb: A small traditional coffee shophouse in the Talad Mai (New Market) area, open for over 40 years, brewing the old recipe full and strong. A classic old kopi-tiam feel — good for a hot cup with a Chinese cruller to start the morning.
items.meta: Traditional coffee · open mornings · Talad Mai area

items.name: Suan Siri Dim Sum
items.blurb: A dim sum shop on Suan Siri Road with an old-school flavour and loyal local regulars. Fresh steamed baskets at friendly prices — a solid alternative when the famous downtown shops are too crowded.
items.meta: Dim sum · open mornings · Suan Siri Rd
items.price: tens of baht per basket · ~100-ish THB per person

items.name: Dim Sum Nak Wing
items.blurb: For the genuinely early risers — open from 5:30am. A varied dim sum menu including seafood options. Good if you want breakfast before heading out on a trip or before your bus leaves, with hot baskets ready before sunrise.
items.meta: Dim sum · open ~5:30am · downtown Hat Yai
items.price: tens of baht per basket · ~100-ish THB per person

blocks.title: How to get the most out of breakfast
blocks.html: Famous spots like Chokdee and Go Yong chicken rice get packed on weekends. If you want a seat and the full spread, go before 8am to be safe. Late risers should pick Gook Chai or Ama, which stay open till noon. And bring cash, because many of the old shops still take cash mainly.

blocks.text: Hat Yai Dim Sum: How to Eat It Like a Local

blocks.html: Dim sum is the heart of a Hat Yai breakfast. Locals call a dim sum shop a tae tiam, from Teochew Chinese. The way it works: sit down, have a pot of hot tea brought to your table, then grab baskets off the cart or order from the counter. A basket usually holds 3–4 pieces, so it's more fun with a group because you get to try more.

items: Har gow — translucent shrimp dumplings, the classic basket to start with
Siu mai — minced pork in thin wrappers, topped with crab roe or carrot
Bao — char siu, custard, or bean filling, steamed soft and hot
Braised pork leg — a standout at many shops, filling with rice
Ha gao / fried spring rolls — crispy fried bites to cut the richness of the steamed baskets

blocks.text: Chicken Rice and Congee: When You're Not in the Mood for Dim Sum

blocks.html: If you're tired of dim sum, Hat Yai still has single-plate breakfasts locals have eaten for years. The chicken rice here carries Hainanese influence — tender boiled chicken, rice cooked in fragrant chicken fat, and a punchy fermented-soybean sauce. Old-timers like Go Yong and Thung Lung are names the whole town knows. Meanwhile congee and pork-blood soup are the hot things to slurp at morning shops in the Kho Hong area — cheap, filling, and easy on your pocket.

items.name: Hainanese chicken rice
items.blurb: Tender boiled chicken, fragrant oily rice, punchy fermented-soybean sauce — a quick, filling single-plate breakfast.

items.name: Pork / soft-egg congee
items.blurb: Hot, well-cooked rice porridge with minced pork, soft-boiled egg, and shredded ginger — warm and easy on the stomach in the morning.

items.name: Pork-blood soup
items.blurb: Clear broth with offal and pork blood, eaten with rice or on its own — a working person's breakfast.

items.name: Chinese crullers + soy milk
items.blurb: The classic pairing with traditional coffee, found at morning markets and kopi shops all over town.

blocks.text: Kopi: The Traditional Coffee Hat Yai Breakfast Can't Do Without

blocks.html: The word kopi comes from Malay, meaning coffee, while tiam comes from the word for an inn — together a kopi-tiam, the traditional coffee shop you find across southern Thailand, Malaysia, and Singapore. Hat Yai sits right by the border, so it took this culture on fully. The traditional coffee here is dark-roasted, brewed through a cloth sock, with sweetened condensed milk, heavy enough to cut through the richness of dim sum. Old shops like Je Chada have been brewing the same recipe for over 40 years.

items: Hot kopi — black coffee with sweetened condensed milk, strong, the best match for dim sum
Oliang — iced black coffee with sugar, refreshing in the hot southern weather
Hot tea / black tea — for non-coffee drinkers, good for cutting the grease of fried food
Coffee with egg — some shops serve it with a soft-boiled egg, an old-style breakfast

blocks.text: Morning Markets: Graze from Sunrise On

blocks.html: If you want a genuine local feel, the morning markets are the answer. Kim Yong Market in the town centre opens from morning till evening, with the fresh-market and street-food zone busiest around 6:30–8:30am — congee, roti, Thai sweets, fried chicken, all great to graze through. On weekends there's Kho Hong Morning Market on Punnakan Road, open Sundays only around 6–10am, and Kong Khong Market, an old flea market with plenty of food.

blocks.title: Straight talk
blocks.html: Hat Yai's morning markets are full of food and fun, but some only open on certain days — Kho Hong Morning Market, for example, is Sundays only, so check the day before you go. Kim Yong is easier to walk in the early morning than later when the souvenir shoppers pack in. And most market stalls take cash, so small bills make life easier.

faq.q: What should I eat for breakfast in Hat Yai?
faq.a: The three things locals eat in the morning are hot dim sum baskets with tea, old-school chicken rice like Go Yong or Thung Lung, and congee or pork-blood soup with traditional kopi coffee. For the atmosphere, graze through a morning market like Kim Yong too.

faq.q: What time do Hat Yai dim sum shops open, and when should I go?
faq.a: Most open from around 5:30–6am, and some sell till noon or afternoon. If you want a seat and the full spread, go before 8am. Famous spots like Chokdee fill up fast on weekends, while Gook Chai and Ama stay open longer, so they suit late risers.

faq.q: Which Hat Yai chicken rice shops are the oldest and most famous?
faq.a: Go Yong Chicken Rice on Kim Pradit Road is the first in Hat Yai, going for close to a hundred years. The other is Thung Lung Chicken Rice, open since 1955, using free-range chicken boiled until tender. Locals know both well.

faq.q: How is traditional kopi coffee different from regular coffee?
faq.a: Kopi is dark-roasted coffee brewed through a cloth sock with sweetened condensed milk, heavier than regular fresh coffee. It's the traditional Chinese-Malay coffee-shop culture Hat Yai took on from across the border. Locals like to order it with dim sum or Chinese crullers because it cuts the richness.

faq.q: Where are the best morning markets to walk in Hat Yai?
faq.a: Kim Yong Market in the town centre opens early, with the street-food zone running around 6:30–8:30am — congee, roti, and Thai sweets to graze through. Kho Hong Morning Market on Punnakan Road opens Sundays only around 6–10am, so check the day before you go.
